categories.definition: Revival, in the Reformed tradition, refers to an extraordinary outpouring of the Holy Spirit that produces widespread conviction of sin, genuine conversion, and renewed zeal in the church, as distinct from man-made revivalism or manufactured religious excitement. Historic accounts range from the eighteenth century Great Awakening under Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield to the twentieth century Hebrides Revival. Grace Online Library gathers firsthand narratives alongside Reformed historical analysis of these movements.

Amillennialism is the Reformed and historic Protestant view that the thousand years of Revelation 20 symbolically pictures the entire church age between Christ's first and second comings, not a future earthly reign. Christ currently reigns from heaven, Satan is bound in the limited sense Scripture describes, and history moves toward one final return of Christ followed by the resurrection and judgment. It rejects both a future earthly millennium and a pretribulational rapture scheme.

Apologetics is the reasoned defense of the Christian faith, answering objections and showing that Scripture's claims are true and coherent. Reformed apologetics, following Cornelius Van Til, argues that every fact of creation only makes sense within the Christian worldview, so unbelief itself depends on borrowed Christian assumptions.

Arminianism is the theological system, traced to Jacob Arminius (1560 to 1609), that teaches conditional election based on foreseen faith, a universal atonement, resistible grace, and the possibility of falling away from salvation. It was formally rejected at the Synod of Dort and remains the chief historic alternative to Reformed doctrines of grace.

Assurance of salvation is the settled confidence a believer may have that they are truly united to Christ and will be kept by Him to the end. Reformed theology grounds assurance in the promises of Scripture, the evidences of grace in a changed life, and the inward witness of the Holy Spirit, not in shifting feelings. It also teaches, against easy claims of certainty, that assurance is normally sought and can be temporarily lost through sin and later regained.

The attributes of God are the perfections of His character revealed in Scripture, such as holiness, sovereignty, love, and immutability. Reformed theology holds that these are not separate parts of God but distinct ways His one simple, unchanging nature is displayed. Rightly knowing God's attributes shapes worship, humility, and confidence in His character.

In the early fifth century the British monk Pelagius taught that people have the natural moral ability to obey God and be saved without inward grace, denying that Adam's sin corrupted the whole human race. Augustine of Hippo answered him with a robust doctrine of original sin, total inability, and sovereign grace that became a cornerstone of later Reformed theology.

Bible study in Reformed practice is the disciplined, prayerful reading and interpretation of Scripture as God's inspired, sufficient, self-interpreting Word centered on Christ. Reformed hermeneutics holds that Scripture is clear enough for ordinary believers to grasp its saving message while also rewarding careful, informed study of its original context and unified storyline.

Reformed biographies retell the lives of the preachers, theologians, and reformers God used to build His church, showing how doctrine and character were forged under trial. They ground abstract theology in real history and give the reader models of gospel-shaped living. Read from a Reformed perspective, they highlight God's sovereign providence in raising up and sustaining His servants.

The charismatic movement emphasizes the continuing operation of miraculous spiritual gifts today, such as tongues, prophecy, and healing. Reformed Christians are divided between cessationists, who hold these sign gifts ceased with the apostolic age, and continuationists, who affirm their ongoing use within careful biblical limits. This list pairs leading charismatic voices with the major Reformed responses on both sides.

Christian Life describes what it looks like, from a Reformed perspective, to walk daily with God after being saved by grace. It covers worship, prayer, obedience, and spiritual disciplines as fruits of union with Christ, not as a means of earning favor with God. The emphasis is on grace-driven, Spirit-empowered discipleship rather than bare moralism.

Christian modesty is the biblical call to dress, speak, and carry oneself in a way that reflects humility, purity, and love of neighbor rather than a desire to draw attention to self. Reformed writers root modesty in the gospel, arguing that hearts transformed by grace, not mere rule-keeping, produce genuine modesty in dress and demeanor. It touches both men and women and is treated as an outworking of holiness, not simply a matter of fashion.

Christian parenting is the covenant task of raising children to know and follow Christ, addressing the heart rather than merely managing outward behavior. Reformed parenting stresses the gospel of grace, family worship, and the biblical promises given to covenant children, rather than parenting techniques or moralistic pressure.

Christology is the study of the person and work of Jesus Christ, confessing him as fully God and fully man, united forever in one person without confusion or division. Reformed theology grounds the whole of redemption in the incarnate, crucified, and risen Christ, who fulfills the offices of prophet, priest, and king on behalf of his people.

Church discipline is the practice by which a local church, following Christ's instructions in Matthew 18, corrects sin in its members and, in cases of persistent unrepentance, removes them from membership and the Lord's Table. Reformed churches have historically treated it, alongside Word and sacrament, as a mark of a true church, exercised in love with the goal of restoration.

Church History is the Reformed study of how God has preserved, purified, and reformed his church across the centuries, from the apostles through the early creeds, the medieval church, and the Protestant Reformation to today. It traces doctrine, revival, and controversy to show God's sovereign hand at work in his people. Studying it from a Reformed perspective strengthens faith by learning from the saints, pastors, and reformers who came before.

Church ministry is the biblical work of pastors and elders in preaching the Word, administering the sacraments, exercising discipline, and shepherding God's people through the ordinary means of grace. Reformed church polity emphasizes plural, biblically qualified eldership and the primacy of expository preaching over pragmatic methods. These books cover both the theology and the practice of faithful pastoral ministry.

Covenant theology is the Reformed framework for reading the whole Bible as one unfolding story structured by God's covenants, chiefly the pre-fall covenant of works and the covenant of grace fulfilled in Christ. It shows how the promises made to Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and David all find their fulfillment in the New Covenant.

Creeds and confessions are formal summaries of Christian doctrine, from the ancient Apostles' and Nicene Creeds to Reformation era statements like the Westminster Confession of Faith. Reformed churches have long used them not as rivals to Scripture but as guardrails that state clearly what the Bible teaches and protect the church from error.

The decrees of God are his eternal, sovereign plan by which he freely and unchangeably ordains whatsoever comes to pass, including creation, providence, and the salvation of his elect. Reformed theology holds that God's decrees flow from his own wise and good pleasure, not from foreseen human choices, and that his providence carries out these decrees in time.

The devotional life is the daily practice of prayer, Scripture meditation, and communion with God through which a believer's heart is drawn toward Christ and shaped in holiness. Reformed and Puritan writers treated devotion as the fruit of sound doctrine worked deeply into the affections, not as an emotional add-on to theology. These works range from short daily readings to deep treatises on prayer, contentment, and genuine spiritual experience.

Biblical discernment is the Spirit-given ability to distinguish truth from error, testing every teaching, experience, and practice against Scripture rather than accepting claims at face value. Reformed teaching grounds discernment in careful exegesis and doctrinal clarity rather than mere intuition or feeling, following the example of the Bereans who searched the Scriptures daily. Grace Online Library recommends resources that train believers to think biblically and guard against false teaching.

Dispensationalism is a system of biblical interpretation that divides redemptive history into distinct administrations, or dispensations, and maintains a sharp distinction between Israel and the church, usually expecting a future restoration of national Israel and a pretribulational rapture. Reformed covenant theology instead reads Scripture as one unfolding covenant of grace, with the church as the true Israel of God. This entry presents dispensationalism's own leading voices alongside the strongest Reformed responses.

Systematic theology is the organized study of what the whole Bible teaches about God, humanity, sin, salvation, the church, and last things. Reformed systematic theology reads Scripture as one unified, God-centered story and arranges doctrine according to its biblical and logical connections.

The doctrine of God concerns who God is: His triune nature, His essential being, and His works toward creation. Reformed theology grounds all of Christian faith and practice in a right understanding of God as revealed in Scripture and confessed in creeds such as the Westminster Confession. It is the broader doctrinal category that includes the study of God's individual attributes.

The doctrine of man considers humanity's creation in God's image, our original righteousness, and the corruption of human nature that resulted from Adam's fall. Reformed theology teaches that all people inherit Adam's guilt and a thoroughly sinful nature, yet still bear the defaced but real image of God as his creatures.

Eschatology is the study of last things: death, the intermediate state, Christ's return, the resurrection of the body, final judgment, and the new heavens and new earth. Reformed eschatology reads these events through covenant theology and the already/not yet tension of God's kingdom, holding that Christ's first coming inaugurated the age to come while its full consummation still awaits His return. It anchors Christian hope in the certain, bodily return of Christ rather than in speculative timelines.

The historic Reformed doctrine holds that unrepentant sinners face everlasting, conscious punishment as just retribution for sin against an infinitely holy God. This traditional view of hell is defended against rival positions such as annihilationism, which teaches final destruction, and universalism, which teaches the eventual salvation of all.

Evangelism is the church's calling to proclaim the good news of Jesus Christ to those who do not yet believe, urging repentance and faith in him. Reformed theology holds that God's sovereign election does not diminish this duty but grounds it, since God has ordained the preaching of the gospel as the very means by which he calls his elect to himself. Every Christian is therefore commanded to share the gospel freely and urgently with all people, trusting the results to God rather than to human technique.

Scripture repeatedly warns that false teachers will arise within the church, distorting the gospel and leading people astray for money, power, or pride. Reformed theology insists that sound doctrine matters enough to name error plainly and test all teaching against Scripture, while urging humility, patience, and love in how that warning is given.

Family worship is the daily practice of a household gathering under the leadership of the father (or head of home) for Scripture reading, prayer, and singing. Reformed and Puritan writers treated it as a God-ordained extension of the covenant, planting the gospel in children's hearts long before it takes root through the preached word. It has historically been considered as vital to spiritual health as private devotion or corporate worship.

TULIP summarizes the Reformed view of salvation: total depravity, unconditional election, definite atonement, irresistible grace, and perseverance of the saints. Formulated at the Synod of Dort in response to the Arminian Remonstrance, it teaches that salvation from start to finish is God's sovereign work of grace.

Free will concerns how human choice relates to God's sovereignty and human sinfulness. Reformed theology holds that the fallen will remains free from outward compulsion but is enslaved to sin, unable to turn to God apart from the Spirit's regenerating grace, a position historically defended against Arminian and semi-Pelagian views of an uncommitted, self-determining will.

The doctrine of God the Creator affirms that God freely and sovereignly made all things out of nothing by his powerful word, distinct from and ruling over his creation. In Reformed theology this grounds human identity, meaning, and moral order, and undergirds God's ongoing providential care and sustaining of the world he made. Creation reveals God's glory and is the stage for his unfolding plan of redemption.

The inspiration of Scripture is the doctrine that the Bible is breathed out by God through human authors, so that its words are fully trustworthy, authoritative, and without error in what they teach. It is the foundation for treating Scripture as God's own voice rather than merely wise human religious writing.

Irresistible Grace, the I in TULIP, is the Reformed teaching that when God savingly calls someone he has chosen, his grace certainly and effectually brings that person to faith. It does not mean grace overrides the will by force, but that the Spirit renews the will so the sinner freely and gladly embraces Christ. Reformed theology holds this grace as sovereign and unfailing, distinguishing it from the general call that goes out to all who hear the gospel.

Justification is the once-for-all legal declaration by which God pronounces a sinner righteous, not because of anything the sinner has done, but because Christ's righteousness is credited to them through faith alone. It is the Reformation's central doctrine, distinguishing being declared righteous from being made righteous over time. Reformed theology insists justification is by grace alone, through faith alone, on the basis of Christ's work alone.

This category covers the Reformed and Presbyterian understanding of church government by a plurality of elders, sometimes called shared pastoral leadership. It examines the biblical qualifications, duties, and practice of the pastors and elders called to shepherd a local congregation.

Limited atonement, more accurately called particular redemption, teaches that Christ's death on the cross was designed by God to actually and certainly secure the salvation of the elect, not merely to make salvation possible for everyone. Reformed theology holds that the gospel is offered freely to all, even though Christ's atoning work definitely accomplishes redemption only for those the Father gave him.

The Lord's Supper is the New Covenant sacrament in which believers remember Christ's death and are spiritually nourished as they feed on him by faith. Reformed theology, following Calvin, teaches a real spiritual presence of Christ received through the Holy Spirit, distinct from Roman Catholic transubstantiation, Lutheran views of Christ's bodily presence, and Zwinglian bare memorialism.

Love and charity concern the Christian's call to love God supremely and love neighbor as self, expressed in practical self-giving, forgiveness, and care for others. In Reformed thought this love is not mere sentiment but the fruit of grace, flowing from gratitude for Christ's own sacrificial love toward sinners.

Reformed theology views marriage as a covenant instituted by God at creation, a lifelong one-flesh union of husband and wife meant for companionship, procreation, and mutual sanctification. Above all, it pictures Christ's covenant love for His church, giving marriage a purpose far greater than personal happiness alone.

Partial preterism teaches that most New Testament end-times prophecies, including much of the Olivet Discourse and the Book of Revelation, were fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, while still affirming a final, future, bodily return of Christ. It is one eschatological position held by a number of Reformed thinkers, often paired with postmillennialism, and remains debated among Reformed Christians who hold other views.

Pastoral ministry is the biblical work of shepherding a local congregation through preaching, teaching, prayer, discipleship, and personal care, following the pattern of Christ the Good Shepherd. The Reformed tradition insists that pastors are first heralds of the Word and under-shepherds accountable to Christ, not professionals managing a religious organization.

Personal Holiness is the believer's lifelong, Spirit-enabled pursuit of Christlike character and obedience, flowing out of justification and regeneration rather than earning them. Reformed teaching insists holiness is both a gift of grace and a discipline believers actively pursue, killing sin and cultivating godliness by the same grace that saved them. It is the visible fruit of a genuine new birth.

Postmillennialism is the eschatological view that Christ's kingdom advances through the preaching of the gospel and the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit until the world is predominantly discipled to Christ, after which he returns. It was the dominant eschatology among many Puritans and later Reformed theologians such as Jonathan Edwards and B.B. Warfield, who read Scripture as promising gospel triumph in history rather than decline. Grace Online Library presents postmillennialism as a historic Reformed option among the millennial views.

Prayer is the believer's ongoing communion with God through Christ, offered in dependence on the Spirit and resting on God's promises rather than on technique. Fasting is a voluntary, temporary setting aside of food that accompanies earnest prayer, expressing hunger for God and humility before him. Reformed teaching treats both as means of grace, not as ways to manipulate God.

Reformed preaching holds that the sermon is the living voice of God, His Word publicly proclaimed so that Christ is truly heard, sinners are called to faith, and the church is built up through this ordinary means of grace. It requires careful, prayerful exposition of the biblical text rather than mere moral advice or entertainment.

Predestination and election are the Reformed teaching that before the foundation of the world God, out of his free and sovereign grace alone, chose a particular people in Christ for salvation, not on the basis of foreseen faith or merit. This is the doctrinal heart of Calvinism, captured in the U of TULIP, unconditional election. It grounds the believer's assurance in God's unchanging eternal purpose rather than in the strength of their own choice.

Prevenient grace is the Arminian and Wesleyan teaching that God's grace works on every sinner prior to conversion to restore enough freedom of will that they are able to freely accept or resist the gospel. Reformed theology rejects this as insufficient, holding instead that saving grace is effectual and particular rather than a universal enabling grace given to all. This category presents both the leading Arminian case for the doctrine and the strongest Reformed responses to it.

God's providence is His continual, sovereign upholding and governing of all creation and history, including the free acts of creatures, for His own purposes and glory. Reformed theology teaches that nothing happens outside God's decree, yet He is never the author of sin, and this doctrine is the ground of Christian comfort in suffering and uncertainty.

The Puritans were sixteenth and seventeenth century English and American Reformed Christians who sought to purify the church of unbiblical practices and cultivate deep, experiential godliness. Their sermons, treatises, and prayers remain a treasured wellspring of pastoral wisdom and heartfelt Reformed piety.

Reformed theology is the system of doctrine recovered at the Protestant Reformation and expressed in confessions like the Westminster Standards, centered on the sovereignty of God, salvation by grace alone through faith alone, and the final authority of Scripture. It traces its lineage through Calvin, the Puritans, and later theologians who built comprehensive, Bible-saturated systems of doctrine. These books range from basic primers to full systematic theologies.

Regeneration is the sovereign work of the Holy Spirit that gives spiritual life to a person who is spiritually dead, producing the new birth Jesus describes in John 3. In Reformed theology, regeneration precedes and enables saving faith, since a dead sinner cannot believe until God first makes them alive. It is monergistic, entirely God's work, not a cooperative human achievement.

Repentance is the God-given change of mind and heart by which a sinner turns away from sin and turns to God in faith. In Reformed theology it is not a one-time act but a lifelong posture of the Christian life, worked in the believer by the Holy Spirit alongside faith, not a human work that earns forgiveness. True evangelical repentance flows from grace and love for God, not merely fear of punishment.

The bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead is the historical center of the gospel and the seal of God's acceptance of Christ's finished work. Reformed theology holds it as a real, space-time event that secures believers' justification, guarantees their own future bodily resurrection, and inaugurates the new creation.

Revelation 20 describes Satan's binding, the reign of the saints with Christ for a thousand years, and a final judgment, making it the central battleground in the church's debate over the millennium. Reformed interpreters have historically read the chapter as amillennial or postmillennial, picturing Christ's present reign or a coming era of gospel triumph, rather than the future earthly kingdom taught by dispensational premillennialism.

Revival is a sovereign, extraordinary outpouring of the Holy Spirit that intensifies ordinary Christian experience, deepens holiness in the church, and draws many sinners to saving faith at once. Reformed theology carefully distinguishes true revival, a work of God's Spirit, from manufactured revivalism built on human technique and emotional pressure. These books study both the history and the biblical theology of genuine spiritual awakening.

The Reformed tradition holds that God created men and women equal in dignity and worth but distinct in role, with men bearing responsibility for headship and teaching authority in the home and church, a pattern grounded in creation order and apostolic instruction rather than culture. This complementarian position has been the majority historic Reformed and Puritan view, though it remains contested within broader evangelicalism today. Grace Online Library presents the complementarian case alongside the strongest scholarly treatments of the disputed texts.

Salvation is God's gracious work of rescuing sinners from the guilt and power of sin through the person and work of Jesus Christ. In Reformed theology, salvation begins with God's sovereign election, is accomplished through Christ's atoning death and resurrection, and is applied to believers by the Holy Spirit through faith alone. It is entirely a work of grace from beginning to end, not something earned by human effort.

Sanctification is the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit that progressively conforms believers to the image of Christ after they have been justified. In Reformed theology it is distinct from justification, a lifelong process of mortifying sin and growing in holiness that flows out of, rather than earns, salvation. It involves both God's grace and the believer's active pursuit of obedience.

Sermons and tracts were the primary means by which Puritan and Reformed preachers proclaimed doctrine and pressed sinners toward repentance and faith, from Jonathan Edwards's pulpit oratory to Spurgeon's gospel booklets. This category gathers classic evangelistic sermons, short tracts, and fuller sermon collections from the Reformed and Puritan tradition.

Reformed theology teaches that sin is rebellion against God's law rooted in Adam's fall and the believer's remaining indwelling corruption, while temptation is the enticement to yield to that corruption. Scripture calls believers to fight both through the Spirit, the Word, and disciplined, daily mortification of sin.

The sovereignty of God is the Reformed conviction that God rules over all creation, history, and human affairs according to His own wise and good purposes, so that nothing happens apart from His will, whether ordained or permitted. This grounds the believer's confidence that no circumstance, however painful, falls outside God's control or ultimate good purpose.

The second coming is Christ's promised, visible, and bodily return in glory to raise the dead, judge the world, and bring his kingdom to its fullness. Reformed theology treats this as a single, personal, public event and calls believers to watchful hope rather than speculative date-setting.

The atonement is the saving work Christ accomplished on the cross, where He bore the wrath of God as a substitute for sinners. In the Reformed view this substitution was penal, definite, and effective, satisfying God's justice and actually securing salvation for all whom the Father gave to the Son, rather than merely making salvation possible.

This category traces the history, confessions, and convictions of the Baptist tradition, especially the Reformed or Particular Baptists who held Calvinistic soteriology while practicing believer's baptism by immersion and congregational church government. It covers the movement's roots in 17th century England, its confessional documents such as the Second London Baptist Confession of 1689, and the ongoing baptism debate between Baptists and paedobaptist Reformed churches.

Ecclesiology is the study of what the church is and how it should function under Christ, its head. From a Reformed perspective, the church is the covenant community of the redeemed, marked by the pure preaching of the Word, right administration of the sacraments, and faithful discipline, governed by biblically qualified elders and deacons. It exists to worship God, build up believers, and carry out the Great Commission.

The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, fully God, who regenerates sinners, indwells believers, and applies the work of Christ to their lives. Reformed theology emphasizes the Spirit's role in illuminating Scripture, effecting new birth, and progressively sanctifying the church, while remaining cautious about claims of ongoing revelatory gifts. He is the one who unites believers to Christ and seals them for the day of redemption.

The law of God, summarized in the Ten Commandments, reveals God's holy character and his righteous standard for human life. Reformed theology teaches a threefold use of the law, to restrain sin in society, to expose sin and drive sinners to Christ, and to guide the Christian in grateful obedience, while insisting the law can never justify a sinner. Reformed and Puritan writers have long treasured the moral law as a gift, not a burden, for those united to Christ by faith.

In Reformed theology the Sabbath is the creation ordinance of one day in seven set apart for rest and worship, carried into the New Covenant as the Lord's Day, Sunday, in commemoration of Christ's resurrection. Reformed confessions, following the Westminster Standards, teach that ceasing ordinary work and gathering for corporate worship remain a perpetual moral duty rooted in the Fourth Commandment, not an obsolete ceremonial law.

The doctrine of the Trinity teaches that there is only one true and living God, yet this one God eternally exists as three distinct persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, each fully and equally God. The three persons are not three separate gods, nor is God merely one person acting in three roles, but one undivided divine being in eternal, personal relationship. Reformed theology holds this doctrine as foundational to all of Scripture, salvation, and worship, since the Father, Son, and Spirit work together as one God to save and sanctify His people.

The doctrine of the Word of God concerns the origin, nature, and authority of Scripture, namely that it is God-breathed, without error, sufficient for faith and life, and clear enough to be understood by ordinary believers. Reformed theology holds Scripture alone (sola Scriptura) as the final rule for doctrine and practice, standing above tradition, reason, or experience. This conviction shaped the Reformation and remains foundational to Reformed and Puritan faith today.

Total depravity is the Reformed doctrine that sin has corrupted every part of human nature, including the mind, will, and affections, so that no sinner can seek God or contribute to their own salvation apart from grace. It does not mean people are as wicked as they could possibly be, but that no part of a person remains untouched by sin's ruin. Spiritually dead sinners must be made alive by God's grace alone, not merely assisted toward faith.

Reformed worship is governed by the regulative principle, the conviction that corporate worship must include only what God has commanded in Scripture rather than what seems fitting to human wisdom. Historic Reformed and Puritan worship centers on the reading and preaching of the Word, prayer, the singing of psalms and hymns, and the sacraments, offered with reverence and joy. This distinguishes it from traditions that permit whatever is not explicitly forbidden.
